title: LangChain: retrievers, splitters, callbacks, tracing
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Document loaders, text splitters and chunk arithmetic, retrievers (k, MMR, multi-query), callbacks and tracing with LangSmith and Langfuse.
source: LangChain Python docs; langchain-text-splitters docs; LangSmith docs; Langfuse docs

questions.prompt: A 1,000-character text is split into fixed windows of chunk_size 200 with chunk_overlap 50 (each new chunk starts 150 characters after the previous one, the last chunk may be shorter). How many chunks are produced?
questions.explanation: Starts at 0, 150, 300, 450, 600, 750, 900. The chunk starting at 900 reaches the end (1,100 > 1,000), so 7 chunks; the formula is ceil((N - overlap) / (size - overlap)) = ceil(950 / 150) = 7. I verified it with CharacterTextSplitter(separator='').

questions.prompt: A multi-query retriever rewrites the question into 3 variants. Each variant retrieves k = 4 chunks, and 4 of the 12 results are repeats of chunks already returned. How many unique chunks go into the prompt?
questions.explanation: 3 x 4 = 12 retrieved, minus 4 repeats = 8 unique chunks. Multi-query raises recall at the cost of extra LLM calls (to write the variants) and a bigger prompt, so dedupe before stuffing the context.

questions.prompt: Chunks are 500 tokens each and the retriever returns k = 6. Together with a 400-token prompt template and a 100-token question, how many input tokens does the final model call use?
questions.explanation: 6 x 500 = 3,000 context tokens + 400 + 100 = 3,500. Raising k or the chunk size grows both cost and latency linearly.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Chunk overlap reduces the chance that a sentence needed for an answer is cut in half at a chunk boundary.
questions.reason: With overlap, the end of each chunk is repeated at the start of the next, so boundary text appears in two chunks.

whys.a: Right: the repeated tail is precisely what protects boundary content.
whys.b: R is the explanation of A, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Overlap has a cost: more chunks and more storage. Typical advice is a modest overlap (about 10 to 20 percent of chunk size) and splitting on structure first.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Tracing gives you a step-by-step record of a chain run: prompts, retrieved chunks, tool calls and latency.
questions.reason: LangSmith tracing is switched on with the environment variable LANGSMITH_TRACING=true plus an API key.

whys.a: R describes how to enable it, not why it is useful, so a is wrong.
whys.b: Both are true: A is the benefit, R is a setup detail, and R does not explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Langfuse works similarly through a CallbackHandler passed in config. Both attach to the run tree, so retrievers, tools and models each show up as nested spans.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter tries to keep paragraphs, then lines, then words together when it splits.
questions.reason: It cuts the text strictly every chunk_size characters, ignoring separators.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true (it tries separators in order such as paragraph breaks first); R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: It falls back to smaller separators only when a piece is still too big. For code or Markdown there are language-aware splitters.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: retriever.invoke('refund policy') returns a list of strings.
questions.reason: Retrievers return Document objects that carry page_content and metadata.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: you get a list of Document objects; R is true, and the metadata is what lets you cite sources.

questions.explanation: Keep source, page and permission fields in metadata. They are needed for citations and for filtering by tenant.

questions.prompt: Match each RAG pipeline part with its job.

right.text: Reads a source into Document objects
Cuts documents into chunks sized for embedding
Trades similarity for diversity among results
Receives events such as on_llm_end or on_retriever_start

questions.explanation: MMR (maximal marginal relevance) fetches fetch_k candidates and picks k that are relevant but not redundant. Encryption is a storage feature, not part of these classes.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about loaders and splitters.
questions.text: A loader returns a list of {1} objects holding page_content and {2}; the splitter method {3} chunks them while keeping that information.
questions.explanation: split_text works on a plain string and loses metadata; split_documents copies each document's metadata onto its chunks.

questions.text: LangSmith tracing is enabled with the environment variable {1}=true, while Langfuse supplies a {2} that you pass in the run config under the key callbacks.
questions.explanation: Older code uses LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2; the LANGSMITH_ names are current. Langfuse: from langfuse.langchain import CallbackHandler.

questions.prompt: Using langchain_text_splitters, create a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size 500 and chunk_overlap 50, then split the list of Documents in the variable docs into chunks.
questions.explanation: Keyword order is free. chunk_size counts characters by default; use from_tiktoken_encoder to count tokens.

questions.prompt: From a vector store variable vectorstore, create a retriever that returns the 4 most similar chunks, then fetch results for the query 'refund policy'.

checks.label: invokes the retriever with the query

questions.explanation: Add search_type='mmr' for diverse results. Some vector stores also accept filter inside search_kwargs for metadata filtering.

questions.prompt: Write a LangChain callback handler class TokenLogger (subclass of BaseCallbackHandler) whose on_llm_end(self, response, **kwargs) prints response.llm_output, then show how to attach it for one call of the variable chain with input 'hi'.
questions.explanation: Per-call callbacks apply to that run and its children. Constructor callbacks apply to every call of that object. llm_output may be None for some providers; usage metadata also lives on the message.

questions.prompt: Use the LangSmith SDK to trace a plain Python function answer(question) as a run named 'rag_answer'.

checks.label: sets the run name to rag_answer

questions.explanation: from langsmith import traceable. With LANGSMITH_TRACING=true each call becomes a run, and LangChain calls inside it nest as child runs.

questions.prompt: Retrieval finds the right document, but the key sentence was cut across two chunks, so neither chunk answers the question. What is the best first fix?

options.text: Add chunk overlap and split on paragraph boundaries first.
options.why: Right: both keep boundary text together in at least one chunk.

options.text: Raise the model temperature so it can fill in the missing half of the sentence.
options.why: Higher temperature only adds randomness and makes invented content more likely.

options.text: Reduce chunk_size to a few tokens so every chunk contains less text.
options.why: Tiny chunks lose even more context and make the boundary problem worse.

options.text: Switch to a model with a much larger context window and keep the same broken chunks unchanged.
options.why: The model never sees the cut sentence if retrieval returns broken chunks.

questions.explanation: Fix the indexing side first: structure-aware splitting plus modest overlap. Then consider parent-document retrieval, which returns the larger parent of a matched small chunk.

questions.prompt: Which statements about callbacks and tracing are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Per-call callbacks are passed through config={'callbacks': [...]}.
options.why: True: they attach to that run and its child runs.

options.text: A trace shows which retrieved chunks entered the prompt, which helps debug wrong answers.
options.why: True: retriever runs appear as nested spans.

options.text: Prompts and outputs sent to a hosted tracing service may contain personal data, so redact or self-host.
options.why: True: treat traces as data leaving your boundary.

options.text: Callback handlers only fire for LLM calls, never for retrievers or tools.
options.why: False: there are on_retriever_* and on_tool_* hooks.

options.text: Turning on tracing changes the model's output text.
options.why: False: tracing observes runs and does not alter outputs.

questions.explanation: Observability is a required part of LLM apps: log prompt version, token usage, latency and user feedback on every trace.
